cards.q: What is a Unique Local Address (ULA)?
cards.a: A ULA (RFC 4193) is the IPv6 equivalent of RFC 1918 private space: not globally routable but practically unique. Its prefix is fc00::/7, and the fd form is the one actually used.

cards.q: What is the difference between fc00::/8 and fd00::/8?
cards.a: fc00::/8 is reserved for future centrally-assigned semantics, while fd00::/8 has the L bit set (locally assigned) and is where your ULAs live.

cards.q: What is the structure of a Unique Local Address?
cards.a: Seven prefix bits plus an L bit, a 40-bit global ID, a 16-bit subnet, and a 64-bit interface ID. Example: fd12:3456:789a:0001::1 is the fd12:3456:789a::/48 prefix with subnet 0001.

cards.q: How does a ULA (fd) compare to a link-local (fe80) address?
cards.a: A ULA is site-wide and routable inside the organization for internal-only reachability, while link-local is one-link only and used for neighbor operations. Both are filtered or never visible outside the network.

cards.q: When should you use a ULA instead of a GUA?
cards.a: Use ULA for internal services such as DNS, print, and management that need stable addresses independent of the ISP, for dual-stack labs without a real ISP prefix, for site mergers (random IDs give low collision), and as migration tooling while GUA grows in parallel.

cards.q: How should ULAs be handled at the enterprise edge?
cards.a: Never advertise ULAs to the Internet; outbound BGP/EGP prefix filtering should include fd00::/8 and fe80::/10. You can route ULAs internally and NAT is not needed, unlike IPv4 private addressing.

cards.q: How do you configure and verify a ULA on Cisco IOS?
cards.a: Configure with ipv6 address fd12:3456:789a:1::1/64, then verify with show ipv6 interface Gi0/1 | include fd and show ipv6 route fd12:3456:789a::/48.

cards.q: Is fc00::/8 available for locally assigned ULAs?
cards.a: No. Only fd00::/8 (L bit set) is locally assigned; fc00::/8 is reserved for future centrally-defined assignments.

cards.q: Can a ULA be routed inside the enterprise?
cards.a: Yes, unlike link-local, a ULA is site-routable, but it must never leave the enterprise.

cards.q: Is ULA the IPv6 equivalent of IPv4 NAT private space that needs NAT?
cards.a: No. You typically do not NAT ULAs; you simply route them internally.

cards.q: Why should the 40-bit global ID of a ULA be randomly generated?
cards.a: A predictable 40-bit global ID causes collisions in designs, so it should be randomly generated to make address overlaps across sites unlikely.

cards.q: What is the full ULA prefix range?
cards.a: fc00::/7, which covers both fc00 and fd00 ranges; if an exam asks for the ULA range, answer fc00::/7.
